title: Ang 296–300: the lunar days
hook: Guru Arjan's poem on the days of the moon
tomorrow: what does a Sikh's day look like, on Ang 305?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ang 269: peace continues, and a lotus that stays untouched in the water. Today the Sukhmani ends, and the moon comes up.

Some people check a horoscope app before a big day; some check the weather three times. Simran's aunt checked the moon. Not a great day for the driving test, she said, by the old calendar. The DMV, of course, had already picked the time. On Ang 296, right after the Sukhmani ends, Guru Arjan takes up the moon's own calendar, the lunar days, one by one. The poem is called Thiti, and it answers the aunt's question.
screen: `HOROSCOPE, WEATHER, MOON.` → `NOT A GREAT DAY, SAYS THE AUNT.` → `THITI: THE MOON'S DAYS.`

segments.voice: In the old calendar, each phase of the moon has its own day, with its own customs and its own reputation. Guru Arjan walks through them in order, and with each one he does something quiet: he turns it toward the One. A day of the moon becomes a reminder of the Name. The weight moves off the date and onto the remembering. That's why the outline's line for this poem is: every day is his. Now the sense part, because this one is meant to be seen. Go to a window tonight and the moon will be some shape: a sliver, a half, nearly full, or gone dark. Every shape is the same moon, lit by the same sun. No phase is the wrong one; the light simply falls on it differently. Thiti reads the calendar the same way. A day isn't lucky or doomed by its number. It's lit or unlit by whether the Name comes to mind in it. That doesn't sneer at Simran's aunt. Her worry is love wearing an old coat. Guru Arjan's answer just points the worry somewhere it can rest: whatever the moon is doing, the day belongs to the One.
screen: `THE MOON'S DAYS, ONE BY ONE.` · `EACH DAY TURNED TOWARD THE NAME.` · `EVERY SHAPE IS THE SAME MOON.` · `LIT BY REMEMBERING, NOT THE DATE.` · then, large: `EVERY DAY IS HIS.`

segments.voice: If you can see the sky, find the moon, or any light: a lamp, a window, a screen dimmed low. Look at it for a few slow breaths without calling its shape good or bad. Let it be today's light, which is enough.
Thiti: the lunar days. Guru Arjan's poem walks through them and hands each one back to the Name.
Your line: every day is his. That includes the test day, and the one after it. Talk soon.

howItsDone: Thiti is read in the Granth's order and sung as kirtan; in Sikh teaching the weight falls on remembering the Name each day rather than on choosing an auspicious date.

notes: v3 storyline (days 1471–1484): Simran is learning to drive in the yard of her dad Harjit's trucking company, with the test at the end of the second week. Bebe Jaswant appears once a week (1474, 1480); Maya, her best friend, comes in and out; paced over two weeks, no overnight turnarounds. Day 1481: her aunt says the test falls on a poor day by the lunar calendar.

Thiti is described only in outline (each lunar day turned toward the Name; the outline's carry 'every day is his'); no single line is paraphrased because the writer could not verify one. A Keeper may add one stanza, paraphrased, with its Ang.
